data.text: Every engineer who has worked near money eventually has the same realisation: a ledger is an append-only log with a very strict schema. Once you see it that way, most of the hard problems — auditing, history, reconciliation — become questions about logs, which we know how to answer.

Before we designed a single table for Ledgerline, we wrote down the rules finance would never allow us to break. There were only four, and the most important one fits in a sentence: every journal must sum to zero.
The same rule also lives in the database as a deferred constraint trigger. Types catch mistakes at build time; constraints catch the ones that slip through at three in the morning.
Never store what you can derive

A stored balance is a cache, and caches drift. In Ledgerline, balances are projections of the journal stream. They can be rebuilt from zero, which means historical balances are a query, not a forensic investigation.

data.code:
select account_id,
       currency,
       sum(amount) as balance
from ledger.entries
where account_id = $1
  and posted_at <= $2
group by account_id, currency;

data.title: A rule of thumb
data.text: If a support engineer cannot answer “what was the balance then?” without paging you, your ledger is storing state it should be deriving.

Nothing in a ledger is ever edited. A wrong entry is reversed by an equal and opposite one, with a pointer to the original. It feels bureaucratic until the first audit, when it feels like a superpower.
The log is the truth. Everything else is an opinion about the log.
